title: Humus

definition.text: The stable, well-decomposed form of soil organic matter, derived from the breakdown of plant and animal remains.

facts.text: Humus is brown to black, made largely of carbon with high amounts of nitrogen and smaller amounts of phosphorus and sulfur.
Its carbon-to-nitrogen ratio commonly ranges between 8:1 and 15:1, with a median of about 12:1.
Only fully decomposed organic matter counts as humus; material still decomposing is detritus, and because the change is gradual no sharp line can be drawn.
Neither humus nor detritus is dead matter: both are heavily permeated by soil bacteria, fungi and other microorganisms.
Humus usually makes up five percent or less of a soil's volume, yet it is an essential nutrient source and improves soil texture qualities.
A humic layer of finely divided, high-surface-area organic matter lies above the topsoil and below the leaf litter; humus occurs mostly in upper soil layers.
Humus is amorphous, lacking the cellular structure of organisms; it retains moisture in coarse soils such as sands and lowers soil bulk density.
The word humus is Latin for ground or earth; farmers also use it for mature woodland compost applied as a soil conditioner.

notes: Soil organic matter#Humus (Foundations seed page) holds further humus sentences (nitrogen 3 to 6 percent, S:2d8a6cdb024c; exchange capacity greater than clay, S:8155ecf69657) for the Foundations pass.

title: Humification

definition.text: The transformation of part of the decomposing organic matter into humus, instead of its full mineralization, by soil organisms feeding on litter.

facts.text: Its raw materials are plant detritus, dead animals and microbes (necromass), the excreta of all soil organisms and black carbon from past fires.
Saprotrophic fungi, bacteria and animals such as earthworms, nematodes, protozoa and arthropods carry it out; earthworms are a major contributor.
Sugars, starches, simple proteins and organic acids decompose first and quickly; cellulose and lignin decompose more slowly, and fats, waxes and resins persist longest.
Lignin, quickly transformed by white-rot fungi, is a main precursor of humus, together with by-products of microbial and animal activity.
Microbially resistant compounds such as modified lignins, oils, fats and waxes are left behind, and new compounds such as polysaccharides are synthesized; together they form the basis of humus.
Reactions with proteins and other nitrogen-bearing products lock nitrogen and other nutrients into humus, protecting them from mineralization.
Early work pictured humification as building polymers resistant to microbes, but recent research shows microorganisms can digest humic substances in redox reactions.
Humification happens naturally in soil and artificially in composting; it can darken soils (melanization) and, for long-term carbon storage, stimulating it beats slowing litter decay.

contested_note: Some authors reject humification as a distinct process, arguing that soil organic matter is a continuum of progressively decomposing compounds.

definition.text: The chemical make-up of humus: very large, complex molecules built partly from lignin and other plant polyphenols and partly from similar molecules made by microbes.

facts.text: Humus is hard to define precisely because it is a very complex substance that is still not fully understood.
In Selman Waksman's classical view, decomposing organic matter looks rough with visible remains, while fully humified humus is amorphous, uniformly dark, spongy and jelly-like.
Under a light microscope, humus may still show tiny plant, animal and microbial remains that were broken up mechanically but not chemically.
Chemically modified polyphenols join into very large molecules, to which proteins, amino acids and amino sugars attach, giving humus a moderate nitrogen and sulfur content.
Radiocarbon dating shows the polyphenolic base of humus, mostly lignin and black carbon, can be very old, while its protein and carbohydrate attachments are much younger.
Microbes strip protein from humus molecules more readily than they break the polyphenolic base, and younger protein may take its place.
Attempts in the 1940s and 1960s to separate humus chemically failed because the extractants reacted with the organic matter and created artefacts.

title: Soil continuum model

definition.text: The view that soil organic matter is a continuum of progressively decomposing organic compounds rather than a set of distinct, persistent humic substances.

facts.text: Because the boundary between humus and other soil organic matter is ambiguous, some authors contest the terms humus, humic substances and humification and propose the Soil Continuum Model.
Its supporters say the evidence does not support the formation of large, persistent humic molecules in soils.
Critics of the humic-substance concept argue that the alkali extracts used to isolate it do not give a fair picture of soil organic matter.
Others hold that humus has distinct properties, mostly from its richness in functional groups, which justify keeping it as a specific term.
The humification theory persists in the field and in textbooks, and attempts to redefine humic substances have produced many conflicting definitions.

contested_note: Soil scientists disagree on whether humus and humic substances exist as distinct materials or are artefacts of extraction within a continuum of decomposing organic matter.
notes: No article of its own; passes the two-page test (Humus#Composition and Humus#Stability, Humic substance#Criticism). The charge-and-nutrient-holding pass may draft the same debate from Humic substance#Criticism: merge if so.

definition.text: The persistence of humus in soil: stable humus resists decomposition for a century or more, while labile humus breaks down within about ten years.

facts.text: Much humus has persisted for more than 100 years because it is hidden inside small soil aggregates or tightly sorbed or complexed to clays, out of reach of microbes and enzymes.
Humus not protected in this way mostly decomposes within 10 years and is regarded as less stable, or labile.
Earthworms, termites and some millipedes form mineral-organic complexes in their guts, so mull and amphi humus forms sequester more carbon than moder and mor.
Stable humus supplies few plant-available nutrients but helps maintain soil structure; effective humus is a ready nutrient supply for microbes, stable humus a long-term reservoir.
Its most stable forms, often called humin, may persist for centuries if not millennia; without new organic inputs humus content declines over time.
Slow oxidation of finely powdered charcoal mixed into topsoil forms a very stable humus, probably important in creating the fertile Amazonian terra preta.
Only humus that gains multi-century permanence through interactions with the soil matrix matters for drawing down excess atmospheric carbon dioxide.
In subtropical and tropical climates, leaf litter and humus are rapidly oxidized and poorly retained because of high temperatures and heavy leaching.

title: Humus and soil fertility

definition.text: The benefits humus brings to farm soils, chiefly better soil structure and a large surface that holds nutrient elements until plants need them.

facts.text: Humus is a negatively charged colloid that raises a soil's cation-exchange capacity, holding nutrient cations where plants can use them and preventing their leaching.
On a dry-weight basis its cation and anion exchange capacity is many times greater than that of clay colloids.
Humus can hold the equivalent of 80–90% of its weight in moisture, raising the soil's capacity to withstand drought.
It increases microporosity and encourages good structure; microbial mucilages secreted during humification glue particles into a crumbly, well-aerated tilth.
Humus buffers excessively acidic or alkaline conditions and chelates heavy metals and excess nutrients, keeping them from leaching away.
Its dark colour helps cold soils warm up in spring.
Whether roots absorb humic substances was long debated; there is now a consensus that humus acts on plants hormonally rather than simply as food.
Some agricultural experts stress other benefits such as disease control, and some judge earthworm humus (vermicompost) the best organic manure.

notes: S:11cf83c1793b is flagged CONTESTED, but the next sentence (S:fb791454364f) reports a consensus, so the entry is not marked contested.

definition.text: The group of organic and mineral-organic horizons at or near the soil surface, formed from organic residues, that characterizes how litter becomes humus in a given place.

facts.text: Five humus systems are described on land: mull, moder, mor, amphi and tangel, found from forests and grasslands to tundras and deserts.
Horizons that may make up a humus form include L, F, H and Ah, but not B or C.
Humus form matters in forest management because it influences whether new seedlings and saplings can establish and the forest regenerate.
Humus profiles (humipedons) change over a few years, while whole soil profiles (pedons) take decades to centuries, because soil organisms drive them.
Most humus classifications are national (French, Belgian, German, Canadian, Russian) and focus on forest soils in temperate climates.
Danish forester Peter Erasmus Müller first described mull and mor, linking them to high and low fertility of beechwoods; Franz Hartmann later added moder between them.
Charles Darwin, a year before his death, published a detailed study of mull formation, which he called mould.
Humus forms of peat bogs and marshes are classified by water-table depth and its seasonal swings and by dominant vegetation, such as sphagnum or herbs.

definition.text: A humus form in which burrowing soil animals mix organic matter thoroughly into the mineral soil, giving a granular A horizon and no OH horizon.

facts.text: Litter disappears fast under high biological activity, so thick organic layers do not build up, while the A horizon of humus bound to mineral particles is well developed.
Mull occurs in deciduous forests and grasslands under mild climates with moderate rainfall, on parent materials rich in weatherable minerals.
Earthworms are its most widespread makers, but Polydesmida millipedes in Appalachian old-growth forests, darkling beetles in drylands and burrowing mammals also form mull.
Plants on mull drop easily decomposed litter with a low carbon-to-nitrogen ratio, which releases nutrients and prevents their immobilization.
More complete decomposition oxidizes organic acids more fully, raising soil pH and base saturation.
A positive feedback links them: better litter quality speeds decomposition and nutrient cycling, which speeds plant growth; mull hosts a high biomass and diversity of soil fauna.
Because its litter is quickly buried and bound to minerals in stable organo-mineral assemblages, mull ultimately stores more carbon than moder or mor.
In HUMUSICA, mull is a humus system with four forms, Eumull, Mesomull, Oligomull and Dysmull, marked by increasingly continuous OL and OF horizons.

definition.text: A humus form, also called twin mull or amphimull, that combines moder-like OF and OH horizons with a mull-like granular A horizon.

facts.text: Its granular A horizon comes from seasonal earthworm activity, and activities at different depths peak at different times of year.
It occurs where seasons contrast strongly: summer drought in Mediterranean areas and winter frost in mountains drive earthworms deeper.
Amphi shows that litter thickness alone cannot identify a humus form: the structure of the mineral horizon below must also be observed.
With two juxtaposed carbon sinks, it may have the best carbon storage potential of any humus form.

definition.text: A mountain humus form on hard limestone or dolomite in cold, humid climates, with a thick accumulated organic layer resting on rock and little or no A horizon.

facts.text: Its organic 'tangel layer', named by Kubiëna, can reach up to 1 m thick.
Tangel and mor are two pathways of organic matter evolution in cold, humid mountains: tangel on alkaline substrates, mor on acidic ones.
Its biology is little studied; one northern Alps study found microbial activity, fungi and bacteria falling with depth while archaea increased.

definition.text: A worldwide morpho-functional classification of humus forms, created in the 2010s.

facts.text: It classifies humus forms from terrestrial, semi-aquatic, cultivated and man-made environments, unlike national schemes focused on temperate forests.
Mull, moder and mor become humus systems (humus interaction systems), each containing several humus forms that differ in the thickness of organic and mineral-organic horizons.
Mull is divided into Eumull, Mesomull, Oligomull and Dysmull, while Amphimull is treated as a separate humus system.
It has been suggested that the pedon be split into humipedon, copedon and lithopedon, in decreasing order of biological influence and speed of change.

definition.text: The sequence of surface horizons used to identify humus forms, following the stages of litter decomposition and its gradual mixing into mineral matter.

facts.text: The OL horizon (Oi in USDA Soil Taxonomy) is recognizable leaves or needles not yet fragmented by animals; it is seasonally absent only in the most active mull.
The OF horizon (Oe) is litter fragmented by feeding animals and mixed with fecal pellets from 30-50 micrometres (enchytraeids, mites, springtails) to 1-2 millimetres (earthworms, millipedes).
The OH horizon (Oa) is humus formed once plant remains are no longer visible but not yet mixed with mineral matter, often made of accumulated fecal pellets.
The A horizon mixes organic and mineral matter, mostly through burrowing animals; macrofauna build macroaggregates over 250 μm and mesofauna microaggregates under 250 μm.
The E horizon is a white or ashy, carbon-poor layer through which water, solutes and colloids such as clay and humus are leached.
Fine roots and ericoid mycorrhizal fungi in the OH horizon can decompose recalcitrant organic matter and pass its nitrogen to the host plant.
The horizons are easy to recognize in the field with a hand lens, along a knife-cut profile or by hand from a small soil monolith.

title: Humus Index

definition.text: An ordinal numerical scale covering all lowland terrestrial humus forms, ranked by the growing share of organic layers in the humus profile.

facts.text: It runs along gradients such as Eumull to Dysmull and Hemimoder to Dysmoder.
Because it can be rank-correlated with soil or vegetation measurements, it serves as an indicator of soil health or forest stand development.
It covaries with soil fertility, forest management type, tree age, pollution level and plant species richness.

notes: Passes the two-page test: the same Humus Index sentences appear on Mull humus#Classification and Moder humus#Classification.

title: Humus form change
article: Humus form#Humus forms in a changing world

definition.text: The shifting of a site's humus form over time in response to vegetation dynamics, land use, pollution and climate change.

facts.text: During forest succession organic horizons thicken, from mull in early stages towards moder under mature stands; in old natural forests mull and moder alternate.
Converting conifer forest to broadleaf brings a shift from moder to mull, while conifer plantations replacing deciduous stands do the opposite.
Organic farming and conservation agriculture encourage earthworms and a mull-like humus form called agri-mull or agro-mull.
Pollution that harms soil engineers such as earthworms slows decomposition and pushes the humus form towards mor, so humus forms offer a cheap early warning of contamination.
Warmer temperatures favour mull over forms with less incorporation of organic matter; a 3 °C rise in alpine grasslands reduced soil humus content.
Rising temperatures speed microbial decomposition, depleting humus and leaving a negative carbon balance in many soils.
Earthworms disperse slowly, so humus forms may not shift as expected; inoculating them to turn moder into mull has given both positive and negative results.

title: Moder humus

definition.text: A humus form intermediate between mull and mor, in which litter decomposes slowly and builds up on the mineral soil, mainly as the fecal pellets of litter-dwelling invertebrates.

facts.text: Like mor it accumulates partly to fully humified material on top of the mineral soil, but unlike mor it is zoologically active.
It is made by non-burrowing detritivores such as springtails, oribatid mites, millipedes, woodlice, insect larvae, snails, slugs, epigeic earthworms and enchytraeids.
It forms under conifers and in deciduous forests where high acidity and poor litter quality keep earthworms and bacteria scarce.
Moder is highly acidic, with high total carbon and carbon-to-nitrogen ratio and low cation exchange capacity, total nitrogen and base saturation, though more nutrients are available than in mor.
Its OL, OF, OH and A horizons are usually distinct; intense animal activity in a loose OF horizon full of droppings is what truly marks moder.
Its thin A horizon is built of sub-millimetre animal faeces, mostly from enchytraeids, rather than the larger peds of mull.
Fine tree roots and their ectomycorrhizal hyphae penetrate the faeces in the OF horizon to capture nutrients, linking soil fauna and plants.
Franz Hartmann described moder midway between mull and mor; HUMUSICA divides it into Hemimoder, Eumoder and Dysmoder by the continuity and thickness of the OH horizon.

notes: S:eb9cb24cd932 says moder has 'a higher decomposition capacity than mull but lower than mor', which reverses the order given by every other sentence (mull fastest, mor slowest); probably a source error worth checking.

title: Mor humus

definition.text: A humus form of coniferous forests and ericaceous heaths in which litter decomposes very slowly and accumulates on the soil with little mixing into the mineral soil.

facts.text: Its litter of evergreen needles, heath twigs and woody debris decomposes slowly because of low pH, low nutrients, high lignin, tannin or terpene content and cool, wet conditions.
Bacteria are inactive at low pH and earthworms are absent, so fungi carry out most decomposition.
A thick OL horizon lies on an OF horizon matted with roots and fungal hyphae, then a variable OH horizon and a sharp change to the mineral soil, with no A horizon.
Instead of mixing with minerals, colloidal and dissolved organic matter is leached through the E horizon and deposited in the B horizon, the process typical of podzolization.
High C:N and C:P ratios immobilize nitrogen and slow nutrient release, which limits plants and yields nutrient-poor litter, closing a feedback loop.
Ectomycorrhizal and ericoid fungi transfer nitrogen directly from slowly decomposing remains to plants, a pathway at its maximum in mor.
Mor goes with very cold climates, high altitude or latitude, acidifying vegetation such as pines and heath, or heavy pollution; some see it as the best strategy for harsh, nutrient-poor sites.
Peter Erasmus Müller, who first described mor, called it beech peat; mor and thick moder were long confused under the name raw humus.

notes: HUMUSICA subdivides mor into Hemimor, Eumor and Humimor (S:446b8c4af53d, S:adde6b87036d, S:f72ace728935, S:9917fae669fe).

title: Humin

definition.text: The insoluble, carbon-based macromolecular fraction of soil organic matter, the most resistant of the humic substances.

facts.text: Soil organic components divide into a soluble fraction, largely humic acids, and an insoluble fraction, the humins, which make up about 50% of soil organic matter.
Humin has the greatest molecular weight and darkest colour of the humic substances, is insoluble in acids, alkalis and water at any pH, and resists microbes most.
As the most stable form of humus it may persist for centuries if not millennia.
Humins are also by-products of sugar dehydration in biorefineries, where their structure and formation mechanism are still debated.

notes: Biorefinery humins (Humin#Humins from biomass sources) are outside soil science; one fact keeps the name's second sense. The CONTESTED flag (S:b141fcb8eaee) concerns biorefinery humins only.

title: Plant litter

definition.text: Dead plant material such as leaves, bark, needles and twigs that has fallen onto the soil surface, forming the litter layer or O horizon.

facts.text: Decomposing litter becomes detritus and releases nutrients, while the loose cover preserves soil moisture, reduces erosion and shelters small animals.
Fresh litterfall is undecomposed and recognizable by species and type; items over 2 cm in diameter are coarse litter, smaller ones fine litter.
Leaves make up about 70 percent of forest litterfall, while grasslands, with little perennial tissue above ground, shed little litter, nearly equal to net primary production.
Soil science divides litter into L (little decomposed), F (partly decomposed) and H (fully decomposed, mostly indiscernible) layers.
Litterfall declines with latitude: fast decomposition keeps tropical rainforest litter thin, while slow decomposition builds thick litter, or mor, in boreal forests.
Litter shields aggregates from raindrop impact, keeping clay and silt from plugging pores, helps rain infiltrate and reduces wind erosion.
Most terrestrial net primary production ends up eaten by herbivores or as litterfall, so litter indicates ecological productivity and helps predict nutrient cycling and soil fertility.
Fires can remove litter completely, and regions with frequent wildfires have sparser vegetation and less litter.

notes: Plant litter#Change due to invasive earthworms (S:dd0f2a46458d, S:3b1559058735, S:b5fd5bafaf08: non-native earthworms in glaciated North America speed litter decay, possibly harming salamanders) is left to the life-in-the-soil entry Earthworm invasions; fold those sentences in there.

title: Litterfall nutrient cycling

definition.text: The return of nutrients from plants to the soil through fallen litter and its decomposition, the main pathway for recycling nitrogen and phosphorus.

facts.text: Plants reabsorb part of their nutrients from leaves during senescence; plants on poor sites reabsorb more, so their litter is nutrient-poor.
Decomposers break litter's simple carbon compounds into carbon dioxide and water and release ions such as nitrogen and phosphorus that plants take up again.
Rain and throughfall leach breakdown products into the soil, adding to its cation exchange capacity, especially in highly weathered tropical soils.
Leaching of iron, aluminium and organic matter from litter drives podzolization, intense in boreal and cool temperate pine forests whose litter is rich in phenolics and fulvic acid.
Nutrient-rich litter decomposes faster, so nutrient concentrations measured by remote sensing serve as an index of potential decomposition rate.
Ecosystem uptake equals annual nutrient storage in plant tissues plus replacement of losses from litterfall and leaching.
Fungi play a large role in cycling nutrients from litter back into the ecosystem.

notes: S:aa36130bf3e3 calls the accumulation of litter nutrients in the topsoil 'soil immobilization', which is not the usual microbial meaning of immobilization; left out.

definition.text: A container or mesh bag set out for a fixed time to collect falling plant litter or to measure how fast confined litter decays.

facts.text: Litterbags are placed at random, marked by GPS or local coordinates and checked at set intervals.
Weighing the dry contents gives litterfall flux: litterfall (kg m−2 yr−1) = total litter mass (kg) / litterbag area (m2).
Under a mass-balance approach, decomposition over a period should equal litterfall input over the same period.
Different mesh sizes are needed to study different groups of soil fauna.

definition.text: The old practice of raking forest leaf litter to use in place of straw for livestock bedding, widespread in Europe since the seventeenth century.

facts.text: The practice peaked in 1853, when an estimated 50 Tg of dry litter a year was raked in European forests.
Combined with other degradation it could promote podzolisation, but if managed well, for example by burying the used litter, repeated removal may not harm soil formation.
Primary forests hold more abundant, deeper and moister litter than secondary forests.

definition.text: The litter layer as a home and food source for decomposers, plants and larger animals.

facts.text: Its decomposer community includes fungi, bacteria, amoebae, nematodes, rotifers, tardigrades, springtails, potworms, insect larvae, molluscs, mites, woodlice and millipedes.
Some plants are adapted to it: bluebell shoots pierce the layer in spring, and rhizomatous wood sorrel thrives there.
Salamanders and caecilians live in its damp microclimate, and the ovenbird needs it for foraging and nest material.
Lichen litterfall feeds wintering deer and elk in boreal forests and sustains mountain caribou through a 'manna effect' in British Columbia.

definition.text: Litter that reaches coasts from rivers or falls in mangrove forests, which follows a very different path from litter on land.

facts.text: Tides, crabs and microbes remove it, and which matters most depends on the tidal regime.
Crabs foraging at low tide can take 80% of leaf material when their detritivory is the main disposal route.
Crab droppings pass undegraded lignins into sediments and water, and each plant species' carbon can be traced from plant through crab to sediment.

title: Detritus

definition.text: Organic matter made up of the decomposing remains of organisms and plant material, and of feces.

facts.text: Detritus is usually colonized by communities of microorganisms that decompose, or remineralise, it; they may be decomposers, detritivores or coprophages.
On land it occurs as plant litter and as organic matter mixed into the soil, forming for example the humic soil beneath a layer of fallen leaves.
Dead remains and feces gradually lose their form through physical processes and the work of grazers, bacteria and fungi.
In forests, detritus by biomass is dominated by leaf, twig and bacterial litter; it shelters seedlings, arthropods, reptiles and amphibians.
Late in decomposition, mesophilic microorganisms break down residual detritus and release heat, the same effect that warms a compost heap.
On land far more material is broken down by passing through the detritus chain as dead matter than by being eaten alive.
As it decomposes on the ground it supplies plants with fertilizer in the form of inorganic salts.
In fresh water most detritus is leaf litter from nearby land, the main carbon source of small streams; at sea it settles as marine snow of dead plankton and fecal pellets.

notes: Humus#(lead) S:1ebfd40751dd draws the humus/detritus line: organic matter still decomposing is detritus, fully decomposed is humus.

title: Detritus food chain

definition.text: A food chain, also called the detritus cycle, linking detritus, the microorganisms that multiply on it and the detritivores that feed on both.

facts.text: Microbes on detritus quickly take up low-molecular-weight proteins, lipids and sugars, decompose complex carbohydrates slowly and build the products into their own biomass.
Detritivores digest mainly the protein-rich microbes and excrete the detritus barely changed; after microbes regrow on that dung over several days, it is eaten again.
Repeated passage thins and fragments the detritus until its complex carbohydrates disappear; bacteria and fungi recycle what detritivores leave.
Microbes take carbon from detritus but nitrogen and phosphorus from their surroundings to build their cells.

notes: Much of the Theory section is illustrated with mudflat snails; the soil food web itself belongs to life-in-the-soil.

definition.text: The large pool of carbon-based compounds in natural and engineered environments, derived from the feces and remains of organisms such as plants and animals.

facts.text: Its basic structures come from cellulose, tannin, cutin and lignin, with various proteins, lipids and carbohydrates.
After an organism dies, microbes and fungi decompose its materials, and the small products can recombine by oxidative polymerization into larger, complex molecules.
In soil, litter that has decayed beyond recognition is soil organic matter, and organic matter broken down into a stable, decomposition-resistant substance is humus.
It moves nutrients through the environment, helps retain water and buffers solutions towards neutral pH, possibly helping neutralize acid rain.
Its molecules range from 200 to 20,000 amu; up to one-third of its carbon sits in stable aromatic rings that are hard to break down.
Measurements usually capture only organic carbon or compounds, so they only approximate the amount of once-living matter.
In water it splits into dissolved organic matter, which passes a 0.45 micrometre filter, and particulate organic matter, which does not.
Equating organic with living comes from vitalism, an idea first questioned after Friedrich Wöhler synthesized urea in 1828.

title: Decomposition

definition.text: The process by which dead organic substances are broken down into simpler organic or inorganic matter such as carbon dioxide, water, simple sugars and mineral salts.

facts.text: It is part of the nutrient cycle, recycling the finite matter of the biosphere; abiotic decomposition works by chemical or physical processes, biotic decomposition (biodegradation) by living organisms, mostly microbes.
Plant matter decays in stages: water first leaches the soluble carbon compounds, soil invertebrates fragment litter into smaller pieces, and microbes then chemically alter the remaining detritus.
In soil its reactions fall into three groups: enzymatic oxidation to carbon dioxide, water and heat; release of nitrogen, phosphorus and sulfur; and formation of resistant compounds that make humus.
Its rate is governed by the physical environment (temperature, moisture and soil properties), the quantity and quality of the dead material, and the microbial community itself.
Decay is slow in very wet or very dry soil and fastest in damp soil with enough oxygen; when dry soil is rewetted many bacterial cells burst, releasing a pulse of nutrients.

Sugars and amino acids are labile, cellulose and hemicellulose (half-life 12–18 days in a temperate climate) moderately labile, and lignin and cutin recalcitrant, so humus accumulates as soil organic matter ages.
Acid soils and clay-rich soils decompose organic matter more slowly, clay binding it out of microbes' reach, whereas tillage speeds decay by adding oxygen and exposing fresh organic matter.
Plant decomposition always releases carbon dioxide and accounts for over 90 percent of the carbon dioxide released each year.

notes: Re-anchored in gap-fill from Soil organic matter#Decomposition to the newly crawled Decomposition article; the soil-specific facts of the old section are kept or listed in mention_sent_ids.

title: Lignin

definition.text: A class of complex organic polymers, made by cross-linking phenolic precursors, that form key structural materials in plant support tissues, especially wood and bark.

facts.text: In cell walls it fills the spaces between cellulose, hemicellulose and pectin and cross-links the polysaccharides, strengthening the plant and letting its vascular tissue conduct water.
Unlike proteins or cellulose it resists degradation, is immune to acid and base hydrolysis, and shields cellulose and hemicellulose from microbial enzymes.
White rot fungi break it down with secreted peroxidases, actinomycetes also decompose it, and under temperate conditions its half-life is about six months.
Reacting with proteins makes it still more resistant, and with by-products of microbial and animal activity it is one of the main precursors of humus.

notes: Gap-fill: now anchored on the crawled Lignin article; earlier facts from Soil organic matter, Humus, Mor humus and Thatch (lawn) are kept in mention_sent_ids.

title: Priming effect

definition.text: A change, positive or negative, in the rate at which soil organic matter decomposes, caused by adding something to soil or compost.

facts.text: It is usually triggered by pulsed or continuous inputs of fresh organic matter, and it usually accelerates mineralization.
The speed-up is often attributed to greater microbial activity fuelled by energy and nutrients released from the fresh organic matter.
Positive priming speeds mineralization; negative priming causes immobilization, leaving nitrogen unavailable.
Fertilizers, plant litter, detritus, root exudates, tillage and drying and rewetting can all prime decomposition.
Where it occurs, soil organic matter turns over at least one order of magnitude faster than in the bulk soil.
Priming appears within days or weeks, is larger in carbon- and nitrogen-rich soils and with larger additions, and has not been seen in sterile environments.
Löhnis discovered it in 1926 while studying green manure decomposition; Bingeman named it in 1953, but it was widely disregarded until the 1980s–1990s.
Its mechanisms are more complex than first thought and remain poorly understood; similar mechanisms may operate in aquatic environments.

notes: Organic matter#Priming effect holds most sentences; the short Priming (microbiology) page (assigned, chunk 05) gives the definition.

title: Particulate organic matter

definition.text: The fraction of organic matter, operationally defined, that does not pass a filter or sieve with openings usually between 0.053 millimetres (53 μm) and 2 millimetres.

facts.text: In soil it is organic matter that still shows its original cellular structure: partly decomposed plant litter, animal faeces, microbial detritus and pollen.
Particulate organic carbon (POC) is the carbon in it; there is typically about twice as much POM as POC.
Most POM turns over in less than 10 years, though less active parts may take 15 to 100 years.
Its decomposition supplies much of the energy of soil organisms and a steady release of nutrients, the amount mineralized depending on properties such as its C:N ratio.
Fungal mycelium colonizing it entangles particles and releases sticky polysaccharides that form aggregates, improving infiltration, aeration and resistance to erosion.
Manure and crop residues raise POM, while repeated tillage and conversion of native grassland to farmland deplete it.
Because it is labile, builds structure and responds quickly to management, POM is often used as an indicator of soil quality.
Eroded, POM-rich sediment from poorly managed slopes can pollute water bodies and cause eutrophication.

notes: Most of the page (about 100 of 170 sentences) covers ocean POC and the biological carbon pump, left out as outside soil science.

title: Soil organic matter fractions

definition.text: The grouping of the non-living organic matter in soil into four categories by size, behaviour and persistence, in order of decreasing ease of decomposition.

facts.text: Living organisms, including roots, make up about 15% of soil organic matter; the other 85% is non-living.
Dissolved organic matter consists of simple compounds such as organic acids, sugars, amino acids and root mucilages dissolved in soil water; it turns over in less than 12 months.
Humus, amorphous colloidal particles under 53 microns, is usually the largest share, 45 to 75%; it adheres to minerals and persists for decades.

Resistant organic matter such as charcoal, charred plant material, graphite and coal turns over in hundreds of years; it is biologically inactive but improves structure, water holding and cation exchange.

notes: Section sits on a POM page but describes all of soil organic matter; merge with the Foundations Soil organic matter entry if that pass drafts the same fractions.

title: Mineralization (soil science)

definition.text: The decomposition, or oxidation, of organic compounds by which their nutrients are released in soluble inorganic forms that plants may take up.

facts.text: Mineralization is the opposite of immobilization, and it raises the bioavailability chiefly of nitrogen, phosphorus and sulfur.
Whether decomposition mineralizes or immobilizes a nutrient depends on its concentration relative to the carbon in the organic matter.
Organic matter reaching soil usually holds too little nitrogen for its decomposers; above a C:N ratio of about 30:1 microbes absorb mineral nitrogen, immobilizing it away from plants.
Carbon dioxide released in catabolism lowers the C:N ratio; below about 25:1 further decomposition releases inorganic nitrogen as ammonium.
Nitrogen mineralizes to ammonium, nitrite, nitrate and nitrogen gases; carbon to carbon dioxide, carbonates and methane; phosphorus to phosphate ions.
Microorganisms convert much soil organic matter into inorganic minerals that roots absorb, recycling nitrogen and other nutrients; the fraction not mineralized is humified.
When decomposition is complete, the mineralized nitrogen adds to the total mineral nitrogen in the soil.
Biogeochemists call the general process remineralisation: organic matter and an oxidant such as O2 yield carbon dioxide, water and simple nutrients like nitrate or phosphate.

notes: The pages for immobilization and the C:N ratio (other chapters' seeds) give the same 30:1 and 25:1 thresholds (S:2c549f525dfa, S:8c29f9ced60a).

title: Glomalin

definition.text: A hypothetical glycoprotein said to be produced abundantly on the hyphae and spores of arbuscular mycorrhizal fungi in soil and roots.

facts.text: USDA scientist Sara F. Wright proposed it in 1996; the name comes from Glomerales, an order of fungi.
It is mostly assumed to act as a soil glue that improves aggregate stability and reduces erosion; glomalin-related soil protein (GRSP) correlates strongly with aggregate water stability.
GRSP declines when arbuscular mycorrhizal fungi are removed from soil or fungicides are applied, circumstantial evidence of fungal origin.
Sampled GRSP takes 7–42 years to biodegrade and is thought to supply up to 30 percent of soil carbon where mycorrhizal fungi are present.

contested_note: The protein has never been isolated, and its origin and role in soil carbon storage are disputed.
notes: Further facts: 1 to 9% bound iron (S:80817487318d), highest GRSP in volcanic soils of Hawaii and Japan (S:af23cb1cf301). Proposer spelled 'Sara F. Wright' (S:b653a2188bd8) and 'Sarah F. Wright' (S:8d6e7fd6dddf).

title: Glomalin controversy

definition.text: The dispute over whether glomalin is a real fungal protein or an artefact of an extraction that also pulls out humic substances and other soil proteins.

facts.text: What exists is a heat-and-citrate extraction yielding material reactive to the antibody Mab32B11, first detected by ELISA in 1987, while the specific protein has never been isolated.
Labs lacking ELISA measure a crude extract, glomalin-related soil protein, with the Bradford assay, causing confusion between ideal protein, antibody-reactive extract and GRSP.
Analysis in 2010 showed the extraction, citrate heated to 121 °C for at least an hour, co-extracts humic substances, so the glue effect may not come from glomalin.

Proteomics shows most extracted proteins are not of mycorrhizal origin, and experiments find arbuscular mycorrhizal fungi can cause net soil carbon losses, so glomalin's carbon role was likely overestimated.

contested_note: Sources disagree on whether glomalin exists as a distinct mycorrhizal protein and on how much it contributes to soil carbon.

sources.title: Mycorrhizal fungi and soil carbon storage

definition.text: Soils, also called arboreal soils, that form where branches, crevices or other features of trees in the forest canopy trap organic matter such as leaves and fine branches.

facts.text: The trapped matter weathers into a soil that can reach 30 cm deep in some temperate rainforests; epiphytes rooting in it add organic material and speed its development.
Older canopies and lower positions accumulate more material, while soils high in the canopy face extreme swings in sun, wind and moisture.
Their distribution follows that of vascular epiphytes, which are far more abundant in southern-hemisphere temperate rainforests that stayed largely ice-free during the Last Glacial Maximum.
They are highly vulnerable to logging and climate change and disappear faster than they can be studied, especially in old-growth forests.

title: Canopy soil nitrogen cycling
article: Canopy soils#Canopy soils and nitrogen cycle

definition.text: The nitrogen cycle within canopy soils, which feeds epiphytes and also affects the fertility of the forest floor below.

facts.text: Canopy soils release nitrogen faster than forest floors, making them a main nitrogen source for epiphytes at different heights.
Their gross nitrification is about the same as or lower than on the forest floor, possibly because canopy soils are more acidic.
Nitrogen fixation in canopy soils depends on environmental variation, especially seasonal changes in tropical rainforests.
Storing nutrients in the canopy cycles them more closely and keeps them from being washed out of the ecosystem.

definition.text: An organism that feeds on dead organic matter or waste by secreting chemicals that digest it outside its body, rather than eating it as detritivores do.

facts.text: Saprotrophic digestion is carried out mostly by fungi, such as Mucor, and by soil bacteria; microscopic saprotrophs are also called saprobes.
Its enzymes split proteins into amino acids (proteases), lipids into fatty acids and glycerol (lipases), starch into disaccharides (amylases) and cellulose into glucose.
In fungi the products are taken back into the hyphae by endocytosis and passed through the mycelium for growth and repair.
Saprotrophs need water (fungi are 80–90% water), oxygen, neutral to mildly acidic pH below 7 and temperatures of 1 to 35 °C, growing best at 25 °C.
Fungi are among the main saprotrophs in ecosystems because they decompose matter efficiently.
Mycorrhizal fungi evolved from saprobic fungi, and ectomycorrhizal lineages arose repeatedly from humus and wood saprotrophs.
Because they recycle nutrients, the Royal Horticultural Society advises leaving saprotrophs in gardens where possible.

title: Forest floor

definition.text: The layer of decaying plant litter and other dead plant matter, also called duff, that mediates between a forest's living vegetation and its mineral and humus-rich soil.

facts.text: In some countries, such as Canada, the term means the L, F and H organic horizons: litter, then visibly decomposing material, then well-decomposed matter whose origins are unrecognizable.
Specialists disagree on whether it equals the O horizon or includes only the humus and intermediate layer, leaving out the litter.
It hosts decomposers and predators, including invertebrates, fungi, algae, bacteria and archaea, and bridges nutrient transfer from vegetation to soil.
Much of a forest's fixed energy and carbon reaches it as litterfall, and its decomposition supplies a large share of the forest's nutrient needs.
Its mass reflects the balance between litter inputs and decomposition outputs, both set by site and vegetation, and the site's disturbance history.

Forest floors are heaviest and deepest in boreal and mountain forests, where decomposition is slow; in tropical rainforests termites and millipedes process litter so fast that the layer may vanish seasonally.
It is also an important fuel source in forest fires.
In one study of Douglas-fir seedlings, removing forest floor debris and compacting soil cut ectomycorrhizal fungal diversity and abundance by 60%.

notes: S:8e6e432250ad (CONTESTED) concerns whether organisms are 'in' or 'of' the soil, a general question not specific to the forest floor; not marked contested. S:eb32db3ca252 (tropical forest floors thinnest except on white sands) carries CITATION NEEDED and is left out.

title: Litter quality

definition.text: The chemical make-up of fallen plant material, such as its nutrient, lignin and tannin content, which governs how fast it decomposes and which humus form develops.

facts.text: Litter with high nutrient concentrations decomposes faster, slowing as those nutrients fall.
Plants on mull drop easily decomposed, low C:N litter that releases nutrients and encourages bioturbation.
Low pH, low nutrients and high lignin, tannin or terpene contents make the needle and heath litter of mor slow to decompose.
Deciduous 'improving' litter goes with mull, while coniferous 'acidifying' or 'recalcitrant' litter goes with moder or even mor.
Tannins protect plants from insects and infection and lower soil pH; high tannin content can lock nitrogen into resistant tannin-protein complexes.
A positive feedback links them: higher litter quality speeds decomposition, nutrient cycling and plant growth.

notes: No article; passes the two-page test (Plant litter, Mull humus, Mor humus, Humus form, Soil organic matter).

title: Dissolved organic matter

definition.text: Organic matter dissolved in water, operationally the fraction that passes a filter with pores of about 0.22 to 0.7 micrometres; its carbon is called dissolved organic carbon (DOC).

facts.text: Soil DOM comes from carbon dissolved in rain, litter and crop residues, manure, root exudates and decomposing soil organic matter, and consists of simple compounds such as organic acids, sugars and amino acids.
It is one of the most active and mobile carbon pools, and affects soil negative charge, acid-base reactions, the retention and movement of nutrient cations, and the immobilization of heavy metals.
Its availability depends on adsorption to clays and iron and aluminium oxides; hydrophobic molecules are held on soil minerals longer than hydrophilic ones.
Leached DOC can reach the water table in well-drained soils, carrying nutrients and pollutants, and under mor humus it moves from the E horizon to the B horizon, as in podzolization.

notes: Gap-fill: now anchored on the crawled Dissolved organic carbon article (which treats DOM and DOC as closely related, DOM being about twice DOC by mass); earlier facts kept in mention_sent_ids.

title: White-rot fungi

definition.text: Wood- and litter-decaying fungi that break down lignin, one of the main precursors of humus.

facts.text: Lignin decomposes very slowly, mainly through white rot fungi and actinomycetes, while brown rot fungi decompose cellulose and hemicellulose and leave lignin behind.
Leaves or needles colonized by white-rot fungi may be bleached in the litter layer.
By cutting the lignin and tannin content of residues, white-rot fungi and bacteria make them more palatable to earthworms, helping form mull.

notes: No Wood-decay fungus article crawled; passes the two-page test (Humus, Humus form, Mull humus, Soil organic matter).

definition.text: The exchange of hydrogen-containing compounds between living and non-living sources and sinks, focused on molecular hydrogen (H2).

facts.text: Biological uptake by soil is the dominant sink of atmospheric H2.
Microbes produce H2 with hydrogenase and nitrogenase enzymes and by fermenting organic matter in the anaerobic food chain; over 30% of microbial taxa carry hydrogenase genes.
In interspecies hydrogen transfer, H2 from fermentation is used by other organisms to reduce CO2 to methane or acetate, sulfate to hydrogen sulfide, or Fe3+ to Fe2+.
H2 is an indirect greenhouse gas, because it can interfere with the removal of methane from the atmosphere.

title: Kerogen

definition.text: Solid, insoluble organic matter in sedimentary rocks, formed from dead plants, algae and microorganisms compressed and heated over geological time.

facts.text: It forms during sedimentary diagenesis and is the most abundant source of organic compounds on Earth, exceeding the organic content of living matter 10,000-fold.
Labile kerogen yields mainly oil, refractory kerogen mainly gas, and inert kerogen no hydrocarbons but graphite.
Type III, or humic, kerogen comes from terrestrial plant matter, from precursors such as cellulose, lignin, terpenes and phenols.
Kerogen and coal deposits are among the sources of natural organic matter in groundwater.

notes: S:0a6d0e451efe gives total kerogen carbon as '1016 tons', apparently 10^16 with the exponent lost; left out. A geology page assigned by the graph; peripheral to soil science.

definition.text: An organism that breaks down dead organisms and releases the nutrients in the dead matter into its surroundings.

facts.text: The term names a role in the ecosystem, not a kind of organism, and is defined by the outcome of decomposition rather than by who performs it.

Decomposers include fungi and bacteria, which digest food outside their bodies, and invertebrates such as earthworms and woodlice, which digest internally and release nutrients in their feces; an organism can be both detritivore and decomposer.
Plants and other sessile autotrophs cannot seek out nutrients or digest other organisms, so they rely on decomposers to free nutrients from dead matter.
On land decomposition happens mainly in or on soil, and decomposers' activity raises soil fertility.
Earthworms and roots first grind and churn the material (bioturbation); further breakdown requires enzymes.
Enzymes for fats, proteins and starch are widespread, so these decompose first; cellulases occur in far fewer organisms and lignin-digesting enzymes in fewer still.

Fungi are the primary litter decomposers in many ecosystems: their hyphae penetrate large pieces that bacteria can only feed on from the surface, and only wood-decay fungi have lignin-modifying enzymes.

definition.text: Compost formed as fallen tree and shrub leaves decompose, mainly through slow, cool fungal breakdown rather than bacterial decay.

facts.text: Autumn leaves are low in nitrogen and made largely of cellulose and lignin, which resist decay, so they break down far more slowly than most compost ingredients.
In damp temperate climates a leaf heap takes one to three years to become fine, dark brown humic matter, worked by a succession of fungi and detritivores such as isopods, millipedes and earthworms.
It is a significant part of soil organic matter in temperate deciduous woodland, and its slow decay gradually returns nutrients to plants.
Though low in nutrients, it is an excellent humic soil conditioner whose structure and moisture retention suit seedling roots.

definition.text: Fallen dead trees and the remains of large branches lying on the ground in forests, rivers and wetlands.

facts.text: The minimum diameter that counts as coarse varies by author from 2.5 to 20 cm.
Saprotrophic fungi and detritivores consume it, recycling carbon, nitrogen, potassium and phosphorus; though poor in nitrogen, it hosts free-living nitrogen-fixing bacteria.
Fungi and other saprotrophs move carbon from dead wood into the soil, a sequestration that can continue for hundreds of years in old-growth forests.
On slopes it slows the downslope movement of organic matter and mineral soil, traps leaves for decomposition, improves infiltration and slows evaporation.

definition.text: The dead biomass of soil microbes, left as cells die and their remains enter the soil organic matter.

facts.text: Microbes cycle soil carbon so extensively that their necromass can make up 30 to 80% of the carbon in soil.
In the microbial carbon pump model, carbon that microbes take up is either respired to the atmosphere or enters the stable carbon pool as necromass.
Necromass is one of the primary materials of humification, alongside plant detritus, excreta of soil organisms and black carbon from past fires.
Pollutants metabolised or immobilised in soil organisms' biomass and necromass become incorporated into stable humus.

title: Brown-rot fungi

definition.text: Wood-decay fungi, mostly basidiomycetes, that break down wood to leave a brown residue that crumbles easily.

facts.text: Wood-rotting fungi are traditionally grouped as brown rot, white rot and soft rot by how the decaying material looks.
Brown-rot fungi attack hemicellulose first, then cellulose, and leave lignin largely untouched, whereas white-rot fungi degrade lignin too.
They are most common in coniferous forests.
Like white-rot fungi, they secrete β-glucosidases to break down cellulose.

notes: The Brown rot page is a disambiguation list of plant diseases; facts come from Fungal extracellular enzyme activity.

definition.text: Any of a group of branched matrix polysaccharides, such as arabinoxylans, found with cellulose in almost all land-plant cell walls.

facts.text: Unlike cellulose, made only of glucose, hemicelluloses are built from diverse sugars, including xylose, arabinose, glucose, mannose and galactose, in chains of 500 to 3000 units.
They make up about 20% of the biomass of land plants.
In decomposition cellulose and hemicellulose are 'moderately labile', broken down more slowly than sugars; brown-rot fungi attack hemicellulose first.
Modern peat is mostly lignin, with 5% to 40% cellulose and hemicellulose.

definition.text: A waxy polymer that, with cutan, forms the main part of the plant cuticle covering all aerial plant surfaces.

facts.text: It is an insoluble, waterproof polyester of omega hydroxy acids linked by ester bonds.
Its monomers fall into two main families, the C16 and C18 families.
Cutan, the other main cuticle polymer, is much more readily preserved in the fossil record.
Extracting humic substances from soil alters ester bonds in biopolyesters such as cutins and suberins.

definition.text: A lipophilic, complex polyester biopolymer of plants, made of long-chain fatty acids and glycerol.

facts.text: Interlinked with cutin and lignin, it forms a protective barrier in plant cell walls whose main job is to block the movement of water and solutes.
In roots it lines the endodermis as the Casparian strip, forcing water through living cells so the plant can select which solutes pass on.
It is a major constituent of cork, named after the cork oak, Quercus suber, and may protect bark from microbial degradation.
Its aliphatic part shares upstream biosynthesis with cutin, and its aromatic part with lignin.

title: Saprophagy

definition.text: Feeding on decomposing dead plant or animal biomass; organisms that do so are saprophages.

facts.text: Necrophages consume dead animal biomass and thanatophages dead plant biomass; animals feeding only on dead wood are sapro-xylophagous.
In fallen plant litter, decomposition is largely carried out by saprophagous soil invertebrates.
Saprophagous macrofauna that digest wood or soil organic matter rely on enzymes of symbiotic gut microflora.
As saprophagous fauna and microbes digest organic matter, its C/N falls because carbon is released as carbon dioxide.

notes: The Saprophagy page separates sessile saprophages from mobile detritivores (S:dedd3abd7c70), while Decomposition treats saprophagous and detritivorous soil fauna as one (S:3fb473e03ba8).

definition.text: The alteration of materials by light, often used loosely for the combined action of sunlight and air.

facts.text: It is partly responsible for the remineralization of biomass.
With biodegradation and flocculation it is one of three main processes removing dissolved organic carbon, often turning recalcitrant molecules into labile ones.
Pesticides are selected partly not to photodegrade readily in sunlight, so that they can do their work.
Iron EDDHA, a chelate for alkaline soils, should be applied in the evening to avoid photodegradation.
